Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-16

Attendees: Jordan Price (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (CTO - Auriga), Luca Morrell (Lead ML Eng - Auriga), Daniel Kim (Product)
notes_summary: Auriga is evaluating embeddings + reranking to replace a legacy BM25 + feature-rerank pipeline. Primary concerns: vector DB integration, throughput (qps and concurrent users), dimensionality tradeoffs, hybrid search (BM25 + ANN) and where Redwood fits (hosted vs dedicated vs private). Security and compliance (SOC2, KMS, VPC) are gating for POC. Agreement to run benchmark and share dataset/sample queries.
autogenerated_topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
transcript_full:
[00:00] Jordan Price: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on this account, with Maya, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Priya Singh: Good, thanks. Excited to dig in.
[00:08] Luca Morrell: Hey, yeah. We have a lot of questions around embeddings and how you handle reranking at scale.
[00:12] Jordan Price: Awesome. High level, can we start with your current stack and the specific user flows you're looking to improve?
[00:20] Daniel Kim: Sure. Right now we run an in-house search service - BM25 on OpenSearch for initial retrieval, then a tree-based re-ranker that uses hand-engineered features. It's slow to iterate and not great for semantic queries.
[00:35] Priya Singh: Also cost is creeping up; our team is frustrated with throughput during peak and we want better recall for paraphrase queries.
[00:42] Maya Chen: Got it. What are your p50 and p95 latency targets? And do you have concurrent users / qps numbers?
[00:50] Priya Singh: For interactive product search, p50 target is 80-120ms, p95 under 400ms ideally. We have about 1500 active users, peak qps around 120 reads/sec for search.
[01:02] Luca Morrell: Our index is currently ~12M docs, mix of short product descriptions and longer specs.
[01:10] Jordan Price: That's helpful. So main consideration is how to integrate embeddings and ANN into the stack. Are you evaluating a separate vector DB or would you prefer Redwood-hosted vectors?
[01:20] Priya Singh: We looked at Pinecone and Weaviate. Concerns are vendor lock-in and cost per million vectors. Also, data residency for EU customers.
[01:30] Maya Chen: On Redwood, we offer hosted embeddings/rerank endpoints, plus Dedicated where the GPU pools are reserved for you, and Private if you need VPC/on-prem. For vector stores you can: use Redwood embeddings and push vectors to your DB (Faiss/Redis/VectorDB), or use Redwood to host and serve vectors for you with managed storage.
[01:48] Daniel Kim: If we host ourselves with Faiss, what kind of throughput can we expect? Like qps for nearest neighbor and then rerank?
[01:57] Maya Chen: It depends on vector dimension, index type and hardware. For example, p50 ANN latency using IVF+PQ on GPU optimized runtimes can be sub-20ms for single-shot queries at 256 dims on an optimized cluster, but if you're doing hybrid (BM25 + ANN) you'll be doing a 2-stage flow: retrieval ~20-50ms, then rerank cost depends on model and whether you run it on CPU vs GPU.
[02:20] Luca Morrell: We're thinking of 768-d embeddings from an open model - bigger than 512 but smaller than 1536. Thoughts?
[02:28] Maya Chen: 768 is a sweet spot: better semantic capacity than 512 with manageable storage. Throughput-wise, 768 dims increases memory and IO vs 512 but not linearly. If you quantize to int8/4-bit for storage and use PQ for ANN, you can reduce footprint significantly. Our Optimize tooling can recommend quantization and batching policies per workload.
[02:47] Priya Singh: Can you walk through a sample hybrid search architecture? We're a little fuzzy on how BM25 signals combine with ANN and then rerank models.
[02:56] Maya Chen: Sure. Common approach: 1) BM25 or lexical retrieves top-N (N=100-1000), 2) ANN over vectors to retrieve another top-M (M=100), 3) union and dedupe -> lightweight feature scoring to trim to top-K (K=50), 4) neural reranker (cross-encoder) over top-K to produce final sorted list. The reranker can be hosted on Redwood runtime; we support warm KV cache to speed up cross-encoder per doc.
[03:26] Daniel Kim: For the cross-encoder, is the model invocation per candidate expensive? We worry about per-request cost if we run a 3B model for reranking.
[03:33] Maya Chen: Yes. Typical pattern is to use a smaller cross-encoder (e.g., 220M or 1B) for rerank to balance cost/latency. Alternatively you can do a two-stage rerank: cheap lightweight model for first pass (like bi-encoder scoring) then expensive cross-encoder for top-10. Redwood's batching helps amortize per-token cost across concurrent requests.
[03:52] Priya Singh: How does caching work? If we have repeated queries, can Redwood cache embeddings or rerank results?
[03:57] Jordan Price: We do prefix/KV caching for generated responses and can cache embedding vectors. For rerank results, you can set TTLs and cache by query signature. It helps a lot for hot queries.
[04:06] Luca Morrell: Ok. A lot of this looks good. But what about dimensionality effects on vector DB size? 12M docs at 768 dims - any ballpark storage numbers?
[04:14] Maya Chen: Rough math: float32 at 768 dims is about 3KB per vector (768*4B ~ 3,072B). So 12M would be ~36GB raw, plus index overhead. With PQ or int8 you can get down to ~10-12GB. If you store metadata and text pointers it's more. We included a quick spreadsheet; I'll share the breakdown.
[04:36] Daniel Kim: Great. Another piece: what about hybrid search latency when you union BM25 and ANN sets? Do we do dedupe client side or server side?
[04:44] Maya Chen: Redwood's recommended pattern is to perform union server-side in the retrieval layer, then dedupe by doc id before rerank. If you use a managed vector store, they usually return IDs which you can join against your primary store.
[04:56] Priya Singh: Security: we need SOC2, SSO (SAML), RBAC, and KMS for key management. Also EU data residency.
[05:05] Jordan Price: We are SOC2 Type II. We support SAML SSO and RBAC. For key management you can configure customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) in Dedicated and Private. Hosted can also integrate with KMS for encryption at rest. For EU residency we have regions and can pin workloads.
[05:20] Priya Singh: For the Dedicated option, how isolated is the compute? Are we sharing GPUs?
[05:25] Maya Chen: Dedicated is reserved GPU pools for your tenant - multi-tenant on the control plane but isolated compute. It's predictable in throughput and better for steady-state high qps, and you can link to private networking for VPC peering. Private is fully customer-managed control plane and on-prem if required.
[05:41] Luca Morrell: If we were to run Private on-prem, does Redwood ship a runtime and orchestration?
[05:46] Maya Chen: Yes, for Private we provide the control plane package and an on-prem runtime that integrates with your K8s. We also provide audit logs and integration hooks for your infra team. There's a professional services onboarding step typically.
[05:59] Daniel Kim: How do you handle nightly re-indexing for vector updates? We update product catalog every 6 hours and need to refresh vectors without downtime.
[06:08] Maya Chen: You can do incremental upserts. For large batches, we recommend a rolling index approach: write to a new index/segment and switch alias after validation. For managed stores, Redwood supports streaming upserts to the vector index and can coordinate with the KV cache invalidation.
[06:26] Jordan Price: Quick Q on evaluation criteria — what's most important for you in this POC?
[06:30] Priya Singh: Three things: 1) latency under load (p95), 2) relevance uplift vs current reranker (we want measurable improvement on curated queries), 3) predictable cost model.
[06:39] Daniel Kim: Also, ease of integration with our existing OpenSearch + metadata store. We don't want a big rip-and-replace.
[06:46] Maya Chen: Perfect. For the POC we recommend doing two tracks: Hosted quick path (Redwood embeddings -> push vectors to your QA Faiss/Redis) to validate relevance; and Dedicated path for throughput/latency testing. If you need enterprise security gating, switch to Private later.
[07:05] Priya Singh: About evaluation: we have a set of 200 prompt/queries for relevance eval. Can Redwood run evals and produce quality metrics?
[07:12] Maya Chen: Yes, we integrate with eval suites. We can run NDCG/Recall@K and surface regressions against baseline. We'll also tie regression alerts to those prompt sets.
[07:21] Luca Morrell: One more: vector cardinality and sharding - if we scale to 50M docs, how many shards and machines would Redwood recommend?
[07:29] Maya Chen: It depends on index type. For IVF indexes on GPU, you'll shard by cluster nodes; rough thumb: 10-16GB per shard for fast ANN search at 768 dims post-quant. For 50M, with PQ and sharding you might land in the low dozens of nodes; our Optimize tool gives a sizing estimate based on hit rates and qps. We'll share that sizing sheet.
[07:48] Daniel Kim: Can you talk cost? Hosted embed + vector store costs vs Dedicated flat monthly?
[07:53] Jordan Price: Hosted is usage-based (per-embedding + per-rerank invocation). Dedicated is committed capacity (monthly/annual) and benefits if you have steady high throughput - predictable unit costs and lower per-token if reservation is high. We can model your 120 qps peak and show TCO.
[08:10] Priya Singh: For reranking models, do you host our custom models or only Redwood-provided models?
[08:14] Maya Chen: You can bring custom models to Dedicated/Private. Hosted supports a set of curated open models and Redwood-verified profiles; for custom model weights, Dedicated or Private is the path.
[08:26] Priya Singh: Ok that's important. We have a proprietary cross-encoder we want to keep internal.
[08:31] Jordan Price: That fits well with Dedicated/Private options.
[08:34] Daniel Kim: A few technical clarifications: when you say batching amortizes cost, how does it affect latency?
[08:39] Maya Chen: Batching trades latency for throughput - we do micro-batching for short windows (5-20ms) to group concurrent requests. For strict tail-latency targets you can set SLOs to limit batching or use dedicated reserved capacity to keep headroom. We also do KV cache warm-ups to avoid cold-start token costs.
[08:58] Luca Morrell: Regarding ANN index types, do you recommend IVF+PQ or HNSW for this workload?
[09:03] Maya Chen: HNSW provides better recall for small-latency budgets but is memory heavy; IVF+PQ is more compact and works well on GPU inference for larger scale. For 12M and 120 qps, IVF+PQ on GPU is cost-effective, but if you need millisecond tail latencies HNSW or optimized HNSW variants may be better. We'll test both in the benchmark.
[09:23] Priya Singh: What's the expected uplift we might see in relevance vs our current BM25+handcrafted reranker?
[09:29] Maya Chen: Hard to promise numbers without runs; typical customers see 15-40% uplift in recall/NDCG when moving to embedding retrieval + neural rerank vs lexical + feature-based reranker, depending on query set. We'll validate on your 200 queries.
[09:45] Jordan Price: Great. I'm going to capture next steps: we'll send pricing, security docs, sizing, and propose benchmark dates. Anything else?
[09:52] Priya Singh: Please include a short runbook for ingest/upsert patterns and best practices for TTL and cache invalidation.
[09:58] Maya Chen: Will do - include patterns for streaming vs bulk reindex and alias switching.
[10:05] Daniel Kim: We'll prepare the sample dataset and share access.
[10:08] Priya Singh: One more question on hybrid scoring: do you recommend linear combination of BM25 score + ANN similarity or learning-to-rank?
[10:16] Maya Chen: Many teams start with linear combination with tuned weights, then move to a learned ranker over combined features. For initial POC linear is easiest to validate. Then you can feed features to a small GBT or neural ranker for production rollouts. Redwood's rollouts support canary tests for learned rankers.
[10:34] Luca Morrell: On the topic of embeddings themselves — model drift concerns. How do you handle re-embedding when model improvements change vector space?
[10:42] Maya Chen: Good point. We recommend storing original texts and keeping model version metadata per vector. For large re-embeds, schedule staged re-embeds and validate against benchmark queries. Redwood's Optimize tool flags quality regressions against stored prompt sets when model versions change.
[10:58] Priya Singh: Ok this is helpful. Can we talk briefly about SLA for Dedicated?
[11:03] Jordan Price: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; we'll share the SLA doc. Private can have enterprise SLAs via contract.
[11:11] Daniel Kim: Are there any gotchas re: GDPR / data subject requests when using hosted vectors?
[11:16] Maya Chen: We provide data residency controls and deletion APIs. For hosted vectors we can set retention TTLs; for stricter compliance Dedicated or Private with customer-managed keys is recommended. We'll include the data handling whitepaper.
[11:28] Priya Singh: Perfect. Any immediate blockers?
[11:31] Jordan Price: None on our side. We'll prepare the benchmark plan and send items.
[11:36] Priya Singh: Sounds good. Let's lock a time for the benchmark session.
[11:40] Jordan Price: I'll send a Doodle and propose the 23rd.
[11:44] [Crosstalk] Daniel Kim: Cool, thanks everyone.
[11:46] [57:30] End of meeting notes: recap and action items recorded above.
